A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SensorLLM. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive reformatting and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original sensor-trend evaluations, human assessments, HAR benchmarks, ablations and cross-dataset experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds CAPTURE-24 evaluations, additional baseline results and model-configuration ablations.

M1.justification: v2 adds evaluated architecture variants: a deeper alignment MLP and SensorLLM-3b using Chronos-base and Llama3.2-3b (Section 5). The principal two-stage procedure, channel tokens, frozen backbones, losses and classification head remain unchanged; these variants do not establish a redesign of the default method.

E1.justification: v2 adds CAPTURE-24 to trend understanding, HAR and alignment/prompt evaluations. Its wrist-accelerometer recordings from 151 participants in free-living conditions and ten activity classes substantially extend the four retained datasets' population and environmental coverage (Section 4.1; Appendix A.6).

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 adds GPT4TS and Chronos+MLP to the nine existing HAR comparators. This introduces both an LLM-based time-series comparator and a direct encoder/classifier control; v1 explicitly stated that it could not include a direct Chronos HAR baseline. GPT-4o remains the trend-generation comparator.

E3.justification: New CAPTURE-24 protocols include a 100/51 participant split, 5% window sampling, downsampling to 50 Hz, 500-step HAR windows and an 8192-token alignment limit. v2 also tests alignment depth and smaller backbones. Section 3 revises the reported task-tuning trainable fraction from 6% to 0.12%, without establishing a rerun or explaining a procedural change. The original four datasets' splits and windowing remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds alignment-depth and model-size sensitivity studies (Figures 3–4), and uses Chronos+MLP to investigate whether encoder embeddings alone explain performance. Alignment/prompt ablations extend to CAPTURE-24. The existing cross-dataset experiment remains, while the second appendix example revises GPT-4o's displayed output.

E5.justification: The main HAR comparison changes from five-run boxplots in v1 Figure 4 to explicit means and standard deviations in v2 Table 2. Both versions already specify five repetitions and report mean-plus-standard-deviation results for ablations and transfer experiments. No increased run count or new significance-testing procedure is established.

E6.justification: v2 adds CAPTURE-24 results, including HAR macro F1 of 48.6±1.14 versus Attend's 43.6±0.55, plus GPT4TS, Chronos+MLP and architecture-variant results. Original trend scores and corresponding prompt/transfer table entries remain unchanged apart from rounding. Example 2 replaces GPT-4o's previously duplicated SensorLLM response with a different response while retaining its 2/5 rating (v1 Table 9; v2 Table 12).

T1.justification: The normalization, projection, training-loss, Chronos tokenization and macro-F1 mathematics are retained. v2 numbers and reformats equations but adds no substantive mathematical definitions, derivations, assumptions or proofs.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain automatic annotation-free sensor–text alignment, competitive HAR classification and transfer across alignment datasets. The introduction updates coverage from four to five datasets, supplying additional evidence for these retained claims rather than introducing a different central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds explicit limitations concerning fixed-class classification and alignment restricted to trend descriptions (Section 7). It also interprets the new encoder control, dataset-dependent alignment-depth effects and model-size tradeoff, and attributes weaker CAPTURE-24 trend results to longer sequences. These substantially expand the discussion of mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 documents CAPTURE-24 sampling/preprocessing, the channel-wise Chronos+MLP construction, alignment-layer widths and smaller-backbone identities. It adds absolute trainable-parameter counts and revises the tuning percentage. Conversely, v1's disclosure that SimCSE's tokenizer was used across metrics except SBERT is omitted. Hardware and code-access information remain essentially unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to CAPTURE-24, Health-LLM, sensor visual prompting and GPT-2, and expands the sensor-MLLM discussion. It removes the PointLLM, MotionGPT, Huang perception-alignment and Zhang survey references. Most related work and the central novelty positioning remain; citation reformatting and publication-label changes are not substantive additions.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten and condensed. Related work gains explicit categories, detailed dataset descriptions move into Appendix A.6, appendix subsections are reordered, and limitations receive a separate section. This constitutes substantial editorial and structural revision beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout and redesigns Figure 1. The main HAR boxplots become Table 2, dataset pie charts become appendix Table 10, and the redundant alignment bar chart disappears while its results remain tabulated. Two new ablation figures and reorganized template tables further change the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support by addressing v1's missing direct encoder control with Chronos+MLP, adding GPT4TS, and testing free-living CAPTURE-24 data. These additions better assess the framework's contribution and applicability. New sensitivity studies, explicit limitations and the repaired qualitative example further improve the paper. The unexplained parameter-count revision and omitted tokenizer detail remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh the stronger experimental foundation.
